e.etymology: The Greek word for night and the name of the primordial goddess of the night in Greek mythology, mother of Sleep and Death.

assoc.t: NYX Professional Makeup, drugstore cosmetics brand

e.note: Sounds the same as nix, to cancel or veto, and as the Knicks.

e.etymology: A recent name used mostly in Spanish-speaking American families, a form of Ailani or Ailany with the -anny ending also seen in Arianny. Its source is unclear.
A variant of Irvin, a surname from the Scottish town and river Irvine, and also the American spelling of German Erwin, an old Germanic name ending in the word for friend.
From Greek Philoumene, beloved. It spread among Catholics after remains found in a Roman catacomb in 1802 were venerated as those of a martyr, St. Philomena.

e.meaning: John (God is gracious) and Paul (small) combined
e.etymology: John and Paul written as one name. Many Catholic families chose it in honor of Pope John Paul II, and American use peaked in 2005, the year he died.
namesakes: John Paul Jones (naval hero of the American Revolution)

assoc.t: Pope John Paul II, pope from 1978 to 2005

e.etymology: A spelling of Annalise, from German Anneliese, which joins Anna, grace, to Liese, a short form of Elisabeth.
e.note: The one-n spelling looks like the British word analyse, and its first four letters invite teasing.

e.etymology: A spelling of Desmond, from the Irish surname O Deasmhumhnaigh, a person from Desmond, the old kingdom of South Munster.
An English place name and surname from Old English beorc, birch, and leah, clearing. The California city and its university are named for the philosopher George Berkeley.

assoc.t: Berkeley, California, home of UC Berkeley

e.etymology: A spelling of Teagan, from the Irish surname O Tadhgain, descendant of Tadhgan, a pet form of Tadhg, poet. Some connect it to the Welsh name Tegan instead, from teg, fair.
A spelling of Aryan, from Sanskrit arya, noble or honorable. The doubled a shows the long first vowel of the Indian pronunciation.
e.note: The usual spelling, Aryan, is tied to Nazi racial ideology in the US and can be misread outside Indian communities.

assoc.t: sounds like Aryan, the racial term of Nazism

e.etymology: In Mexican and Mexican American families it is taken from Nahuatl icel, alone or only one. Izel is also a separate Turkish name.
A spelling of Finley, from Scottish Gaelic Fionnlagh, built from fionn, fair or white, and laoch, warrior.

e.meaning: pomegranate in Uzbek; honor as a form of Annora
e.etymology: Two names share the spelling: an Uzbek name from anor, pomegranate, and a variant of Annora, a medieval English form of Honora, honor. It rose after the film Anora won the 2025 Best Picture Oscar.

assoc.t: Anora, 2024 film that won the Best Picture Oscar

e.note: The title character of the 2024 film Anora is a Brooklyn stripper and sex worker, and many adults now connect the name with her.

e.etymology: A Bosnian name, the feminine of Amil, which is of Arabic origin. In the US it also appeals as a blend of Amelia and Mila.
A feminine elaboration of azure, the blue of a clear sky. The word came through French and Arabic from Persian lajevard, lapis lazuli.

assoc.t: Azura, a Daedric Prince in The Elder Scrolls games

e.etymology: A recent Spanish-language coinage that joins Santi-, as in Santiago and Santino (from santo, saint), to the -iel ending of Daniel, Yadiel and Jadiel.
From Hebrew ednah, pleasure or delight, related to Eden. Edna appears in the Book of Tobit, and in Ireland the name also served as an English form of Eithne. It was a top American name around 1900.
namesakes: Edna Krabappel (Bart's teacher on The Simpsons)

assoc.t: Edna Mode, the designer in Pixar's The Incredibles

e.etymology: An English place name and surname from Old English clif, cliff or slope, and tun, settlement. It was most used as a first name in the early 1900s.
The English word lovely, from Old English luflic, used as a given name. It is also an established girl's name in the Philippines.
An English place name and surname, from the Old English personal name Ella (or the word for eel) with -ing and tun, settlement. Most Americans know it from jazz composer Duke Ellington.

assoc.t: Duke Ellington, jazz composer and bandleader

e.etymology: A Persian name from zar, gold; zari is also the word for gold-thread brocade. In the US it doubles as a short form of Zaria and Zariah.
The everyday Hawaiian form of Matthew; the Hawaiian Bible spells it Mataio. Matthew goes back to Hebrew Mattityahu, gift of God.

e.meaning: pure, the traditional reading of Catherine
e.etymology: From Irish Caitlin, a form of Catherine that came through Old French Cateline. In Irish it sounds like kat-LEEN, the source of Kathleen; KAYT-lin arose in the 1970s from reading the Irish spelling as English.
In the Bible Dan is a son of Jacob and the founder of one of the twelve tribes; the name means he judged. Most American Dans are short for Daniel, God is my judge.
namesakes: Dan Marino (Hall of Fame Dolphins quarterback)
Dan Aykroyd (Ghostbusters and Blues Brothers actor)

e.etymology: A spelling of Jocelyn with the -lynn ending. Jocelyn was a Norman men's name, from a Germanic name based on the tribal name of the Gauts; it became a women's name in the 20th century.
From Arabic samiya, the feminine of sami, high or exalted.
A spelling of Presley, an English surname from Old English preost, priest, and leah, clearing. The surname is famous from Elvis Presley.

assoc.t: Elvis Presley, the King of Rock and Roll (as Presley)

e.etymology: The Scandinavian form of Caspar and Jasper, the name tradition gives to one of the three Magi. It is usually traced to an Old Persian word for treasurer.
A pet form of Olivia, made by dropping the first syllable and adding -y. Olivia comes from Latin oliva, olive, and was made familiar by Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.
namesakes: Livvy Dunne (LSU gymnast and social media star)

e.etymology: The English word for a jeweled crown, from Latin and Greek tiara, first the name of a Persian headdress. It came into use as an American girl's name in the 1980s and peaked in the 1990s.
An American first name taken from the surname Olin, in use since the 1800s and most common around 1900. The surname's origin is unclear; Olin is also a Swedish family name.

e.meaning: title of respect for a man or a knight
e.etymology: The English title for a knight and the polite form of address for a man, a shortening of sire, from Old French and Latin senior, elder. Beyonce and Jay-Z named their son Sir in 2017.

assoc.t: sir, the everyday polite form of address for a man

e.note: It is a form of address, so introductions, forms and roll calls will cause double takes.
